COOLING PROBLEMS

When a Heat Pump Stops Cooling Properly

A heat pump cooling problem can begin at the controls, airflow path, or refrigerant circuit. The same warm room can have several causes. These signs help describe the problem when requesting service; safe observations do not replace a diagnosis.

Warm air with the thermostat set to cool Call today

Likely causes

  • Thermostat mode or control setting
  • Restricted indoor airflow
  • Refrigerant or reversing valve fault

Check safely first

  • Confirm the displayed mode is cool.
  • Check the accessible filter without opening equipment panels.
  • Note whether the problem followed a switch from heating.

What the technician does

A technician measures supply-to-return air temperature, checks airflow, and compares refrigerant pressures with operating conditions. Valve control voltage and pipe temperatures distinguish a mode-change fault. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Request service today; appointment timing depends on the schedule.

Likely causes

  • Dirty filter or blocked return path
  • Reduced heat transfer at the outdoor unit
  • Refrigerant loss or an equipment mismatch

Check safely first

  • Check for a visibly dirty filter.
  • Keep supply and return grilles clear of furniture.
  • Record which rooms stay warm and when the problem occurs.

What the technician does

A technician measures airflow and the indoor temperature drop, then checks outdoor coil condition and refrigerant pressures. These readings distinguish restricted heat transfer from a charge problem. Book an assessment if cooling remains weak after safe checks.

Ice appears on the refrigerant line or indoor coil Call today

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow across the evaporator coil
  • Refrigerant problem
  • Control or airflow fault

Check safely first

  • Stop cooling at the thermostat.
  • Inspect the accessible filter only.
  • Observe visible ice without removing panels.
  • Leave the ice to thaw; do not chip it.

What the technician does

After the ice thaws, a technician measures airflow across the evaporator coil and checks refrigerant pressures and line temperatures. Those readings separate a restriction from a charge or control fault. Stop cooling now and request service; repair time depends on the cause.

Heat Pump Cooling Service Questions

Why does a heat pump blow warm air in cooling mode?

Warm air can reflect a thermostat setting, restricted airflow, a refrigerant problem, or a reversing valve that has not changed modes. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. A service request should include whether the problem began after a mode change or developed during steady summer operation.

Does a heat pump need refrigerant added every summer?

A heat pump should not need a routine summer refrigerant refill. Low refrigerant calls for an assessment of the cause, including a possible leak. Adding refrigerant without addressing the cause can leave the cooling problem unresolved. The refrigerant type and repair scope affect the next steps.

Can a reversing valve problem look like an AC failure?

Yes. A heat pump uses a reversing valve to change the direction of refrigerant flow between heating and cooling. A control problem or valve fault can prevent that change. Warm airflow alone does not identify a failed valve; the settings, airflow, and operating conditions also need attention.

Can central AC be replaced with a heat pump?

A ducted heat pump can be considered when replacing central AC, but the indoor equipment, controls, and ducts must suit the proposed system. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment. A replacement discussion should distinguish the cooling project from the separate plan for winter heating.

What should a summer heat pump service request include?

Useful details include the model, current thermostat mode, rooms affected, visible ice or water, and when cooling last worked normally. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows. Roof access or locked equipment areas should be mentioned when arranging a visit.

Is heat pump maintenance the same as AC maintenance?

The cooling side shares airflow, heat-transfer, and drainage concerns with an air conditioner. A heat pump also changes between cooling and heating modes. Seasonal service should account for the complete system. City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch, and member discounts.

Should a frozen heat pump keep running to cool the home?

Continued cooling operation can add ice and reduce airflow further. Stop cooling and arrange service rather than chipping ice or handling refrigerant connections. A homeowner can note the filter condition and blocked vents. Ice alone does not prove that refrigerant is low or identify the repair needed.

Poor cooling alone does not justify replacement. A correctable airflow or control issue differs from recurring refrigerant leaks or several major faults. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Heat pump cooling in Chicago: service, repair and summer performance

By the City & Suburban team · Reviewed by Rob, owner of City & Suburban · Updated October 2026 · 18 min read

A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run in reverse. In summer it cools a Chicago home the way central air does, through the same compressor, the same coils and the same ductwork. That shared hardware is why a heat pump which stops cooling in July is a cooling problem, not a heating problem. It is also why the summer faults are specific: a reversing valve that will not shift, a charge that was set in the wrong mode, a defrost board that holds the outdoor fan off. This guide covers what a heat pump needs in cooling season, what Chicago buildings allow, and what switching from central air to a heat pump really changes.

Key takeaways

  • In cooling mode a heat pump is an air conditioner: same compressor, same refrigerant, same ductwork, with a reversing valve added.
  • Warm air in summer usually means one of three things: a stuck reversing valve, a low refrigerant charge, or a control signal that never called for cooling.
  • A heat pump never gets an idle season and runs more hours heating than cooling, so it needs service twice a year.
  • Charge accuracy matters more on a heat pump, because the same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions.
  • City & Suburban repairs heat pumps of all makes and models, installs American Standard equipment, and measures before quoting a part.

How does a heat pump cool a Chicago home in summer?

SHORT ANSWER

In cooling mode a heat pump works like central air. The compressor moves refrigerant, the indoor coil takes heat out of house air, and the outdoor coil dumps that heat outside. The one extra part is a reversing valve, which sets the direction of flow. That valve, the charge and the airflow all have to be tested on a summer call, because all three can look like a dead compressor. City & Suburban repairs heat pumps of all makes and models.

Most Chicago homes with a heat pump got one the same way. An older system came out, and a heat pump went back in on the same pad. Some condos and gut rehabs added cooling where no gas line was available. Either way the outdoor unit sits where the old equipment sat, often on a flat roof or in a narrow side yard between two buildings.

The usual summer call starts with a homeowner who assumes a heat pump is a heating machine. So the search is for a heating company. A technician arrives, checks the indoor furnace side, finds nothing wrong and leaves a service charge behind. Meanwhile the real fault sits in a cooling circuit that nobody measured. Two visits get billed for one problem.

What changed is that the heating and cooling sides are no longer separate boxes. One compressor, one charge and one coil set now serve both seasons, so a summer symptom can come from a winter part. A defrost board that fails stuck can hold the outdoor fan off in July. A valve solenoid that sticks halfway sends some hot gas back indoors. Neither part exists on a plain air conditioner.

A no-cooling heat pump call is a refrigeration diagnosis first. The order that works confirms the mode, then reads suction and liquid pressure. Superheat, subcooling and the temperature drop across the indoor coil follow. Those four numbers separate a valve fault from a charge fault from an airflow fault. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models and gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees, so the part is named once the readings agree.

Cook County Assessor records for the eight Chicago townships show 133,080 houses and small multi-family buildings with central air, and 306,261 without it. Cooling is the newer system in most of this housing stock. A heat pump is the version that lands where a second machine will not fit, so heat pump work here is mostly retrofit work.

Why would a heat pump blow warm air in the middle of summer?

SHORT ANSWER

Warm air from a heat pump in July has three common causes. The reversing valve never shifted into cooling, the refrigerant charge is low, or the control signal asked for heat. The first check belongs at the valve itself. A system stuck in heating will run, draw normal current and sound fine while it quietly warms the house. City & Suburban repairs heat pumps of all makes and models.

The call tends to come on the first hot weekend. The thermostat reads 78 degrees, the outdoor unit is running, and air is moving at the registers. That air is room temperature or warmer, and nothing sounds broken. In a Lincoln Park condo with a rooftop unit, the homeowner often cannot even see the equipment to tell whether it is running at all.

The common response is to add refrigerant. A low charge does cause weak cooling, so gauges go on, gas goes in, and the system cools a little better for a week. Nothing was leak tested and nothing was weighed. The charge is now wrong in both modes, which costs the homeowner a second visit and a compressor working harder than it should.

The mechanism most often missed is where the valve rests. On nearly every home heat pump the valve is powered for one mode and relaxed for the other, and the maker decides which. A failed solenoid coil, a broken control wire or a thermostat set up as a conventional system leaves the valve in its resting state. The machine then heats on a cooling call, quite happily.

A sound test checks the signal and the valve separately. Thermostat output gets read at the equipment first, then the solenoid is powered by hand so the slide can be heard and felt shifting. Pipe temperatures either side of the valve body confirm the change. That order separates a thermostat problem from a wiring problem from a mechanical one, and only the last needs a part. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, and the same readings apply on any air conditioner repair call.

Nisha J. described that order of work in June 2026. The review says "Rob investigated the issue carefully and quickly found a refrigerant leak". The next line reads, "He recommended a cost-effective solution and didn't try to charge us for things we didn't need." Finding the leak before adding gas is what separates a repair from a refill.

  • Thermostat set to heat, or configured for a conventional system instead of a heat pump
  • Reversing valve solenoid coil burned out, so the valve stays in its resting mode
  • Control wire to the valve broken at the outdoor unit, a common spot for ice and yard damage
  • Low refrigerant charge from a leak at a coil joint, a service valve or the line set
  • Outdoor fan not running, so the heat pulled from the house has nowhere to go
  • Dirty indoor coil or a clogged filter, which drops airflow and capacity together

What goes wrong with a reversing valve, and how is one tested?

SHORT ANSWER

A reversing valve fails in three ways. The solenoid coil dies, the inner slide sticks between positions, or the valve leaks hot gas across its own ports. All three are worth testing before the part is quoted, since the valve body is brazed into the line set. Replacing one means recovering the charge, cutting the unit open and starting again on vacuum. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting and repairs all makes and models.

The valve sits on the outdoor unit, a brass cylinder about the size of a fist, with four copper tubes and a small coil on top. Chicago weather is hard on it. Road salt, standing water at a flat roof drain and ten winters of freeze and thaw all work on the coil and its wiring. Winter performance and backup heat sit on the heat pumps page; summer faults are the subject here.

A valve is often condemned on symptoms alone. The system does not cool, the valve is the exotic part, so a quote appears for a valve and a full charge. If the slide was only sticking, the real fault was dirt or a pressure imbalance. The new valve will stick too, and the homeowner has paid for refrigerant twice.

A sticking slide moves on pressure difference, not on magnetism. The solenoid shifts a small pilot valve, and the pressure the compressor makes does the real work. So a weak compressor, a low charge or a restriction can leave a healthy valve halfway across. The test has to separate magnetic force from pressure, which is why the order of checks matters more than the parts list.

The coil gets checked for resistance and for a magnetic field with the circuit live. A light tap on the valve body while the system runs shows whether the slide completes its travel. A valve that bypasses internally sends hot discharge gas straight into the suction port. The common suction line then runs abnormally warm, within a few degrees of the discharge line, while the coil-to-valve tube stays cold. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting, so a valve is replaced only when those readings condemn it, and the charge is weighed back in afterward.

Karam R. wrote in December 2025 that Rob is "the most honest person I have worked with in more than 20 years." Testing a valve before condemning it is where that shows up on a sealed system. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models and backs the work with a satisfaction guarantee.

Pro tip: A valve that shifts only once the system is warm, or only after a tap, is already failing. Scheduling that replacement outside a heat wave costs less than doing it twice.

Why does refrigerant charge matter more on a heat pump than on an air conditioner?

SHORT ANSWER

The same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions, so a heat pump has less room for a wrong charge. Weighing refrigerant in beats topping off by pressure, and superheat and subcooling confirm the result in the mode the system is running. A charge set by feel in one season reads wrong in the other. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting.

A Chicago heat pump runs far more hours heating than cooling, and it never gets an idle season. The outdoor coil is a condenser in July and an evaporator in January. The indoor evaporator coil swaps roles the same way. Every joint in that circuit sees both pressure extremes and both temperature extremes, year after year.

Charging by pressure alone is still common. Gauges go on, the numbers get compared to a sticker, and gas is added until the suction pressure looks familiar. That method tolerates some error on a cooling-only system. On a heat pump it stacks two errors, because the metering device and the accumulator behave differently in each mode.

The part most often skipped is the path refrigerant takes in reverse. A heat pump carries extra check valves to route flow around the metering device when the mode changes. A stuck check valve, a plugged distributor or a blocked filter drier reads like a charge problem while the charge is correct. Adding gas then makes the numbers worse, not better.

Correct practice recovers the charge, weighs it, and recharges to the amount the maker states, with the leak found before any gas goes in. Line length is added to the factory charge at the published rate, which matters on rooftop and side yard installs with a long line set. Written readings let the next visit start from a known number. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, and a charge check belongs to an AC tune-up on a heat pump too.

Refrigerant work is also the least documented part of the trade. A City of Chicago permit is required to replace equipment, but repair, diagnosis, maintenance and refrigerant work need none. Of 62,810 permits issued in the 24 months to August 2026, only 4,888 mention HVAC work at all. Nothing outside the shop's own method checks a charge, which is why the numbers belong on the invoice.

Pro tip: A charge that was topped off instead of weighed in is worth correcting early in cooling season. Recovering and recharging to weight takes one visit and removes a variable from every repair after it.

What should a heat pump service call include in cooling season?

SHORT ANSWER

A cooling season heat pump visit should cover both halves of the machine. That means mode and valve operation, charge by measurement, airflow across the indoor coil, electrical draw, and the defrost control that only runs in winter. A thorough visit works through that whole list instead of stopping at the first fault. City & Suburban gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees before any part is ordered.

From the driveway, a heat pump call in August looks like an air conditioning call. The difference is in what gets left alone. A cooling-only visit never touches a defrost board, an outdoor sensor or a backup heat relay, because those parts are not there. A heat pump paired with an air handler has no gas side at all, so the whole visit is refrigeration and electrical.

Many summer visits stop at the first fault that explains the symptom. A dirty filter gets changed, cooling comes back, and the invoice closes. Three weeks later the capacitor that was already reading low takes the compressor off line during a heat wave. The second call costs more than the first, and it arrives at the worst time of the year.

What changes the math is run hours. A cooling-only system in Chicago runs a few hundred hours a year. A heat pump runs in both seasons, so the compressor, contactor, capacitor and outdoor fan motor age at roughly twice the rate. Parts that would have outlived an air conditioner now wear out mid life, which makes the electrical readings as important as the refrigerant ones.

The electrical half of the visit measures compressor and fan amps against the nameplate. The capacitor gets tested under load, and the contactor is checked for pitted contacts. Forcing the defrost cycle in cooling season proves the board, the sensor and the valve before winter. How often does a heat pump need service when it runs all year?

SHORT ANSWER

A heat pump should be serviced twice a year, once before cooling season and once before heating season. It builds up roughly double the run hours of a cooling-only system. City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch and member discounts, and the spring visit is the one that catches summer faults while the weather is still mild.

An air conditioner in Chicago gets one tune-up in spring and then sits idle for seven months. A heat pump never sits idle. It switches modes in October and again in April. The outdoor coil collects cottonwood in May, grass clippings in July and leaves in November, so the cabinet is never clean for long.

The default is to treat the machine as an air conditioner and book one spring visit. That visit washes the outdoor coil, checks the charge and closes. Everything that only runs in heating mode goes unchecked for a full year, so the first cold night becomes the test. A no heat call in January costs more than a scheduled hour in April.

The better split is by mode rather than by season name. A spring visit has to prove cooling capacity and clear the condensate path. A fall visit has to prove the defrost cycle, the backup heat staging and the valve in its winter position. One system, two checklists, because it is really two machines in one cabinet.

A two visit cycle fits the machine. Filters are sized and changed at each visit, the outdoor coil is washed from the inside out, and the charge is verified rather than assumed. Plan members at City & Suburban get seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch and member discounts, and the same maintenance plans cover furnaces and air conditioners.

Enrique G. described that pattern in June 2025, writing, "I have been using City & Suburban (Rob) for 8yrs just for maintenance and he has been great every time." The same review says the company later installed the replacement air conditioner.

  • Fall: defrost cycle forced, defrost sensor and board confirmed, valve proven in its heating position
  • Fall: backup heat staging checked, so it does not run alongside the compressor

Should a Chicago home replace central air with a heat pump?

SHORT ANSWER

Replacing a failed air conditioner with a heat pump costs more up front and changes almost nothing about summer comfort, because the cooling side is the same. The reason to do it is heating. A sound quote prices the heat pump and the straight swap side by side, at the same capacity and the same scope. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees.

The decision usually arrives when the outdoor unit dies. A Chicago home with a furnace in the basement and an air conditioner on a pad or a flat roof has two choices at that moment. One is a straight air conditioner swap. The other is a heat pump on the same pad, wired to the same blower, with the furnace kept for the coldest weather.

The usual quote compares equipment prices and stops there. A heat pump costs more than an air conditioner of the same capacity, so the cheaper line wins and the conversation ends. What that leaves out is the electrical work, the control changes and the running cost across a full year. The decision actually sits in those three items.

The mechanism that makes the swap practical is the furnace itself. A heat pump paired with an existing gas furnace runs as a dual-fuel system. The compressor carries mild weather, and the furnace takes over below a set outdoor temperature. That crossover point is the balance point, and it decides running cost. It sets how many hours run on the electric rate and how many on the gas rate. Rated efficiency and whether the compressor stages fill in the rest, and nothing about the ducts or the summer operation changes.

The comparison that helps is like for like: the heat pump quote and the AC replacement quote at matched capacity and scope. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment, repairs all makes and models, and offers financing through Wells Fargo Home Projects, subject to credit approval. Panel capacity, breaker size and the disconnect belong in that quote, since the unit now carries a winter load as well as a summer one. Rebates and tax credits for heat pumps shift from year to year. Ask which programs are in force at the time of the quote.

City permit records show how uncommon the swap still is here. Of those, 27 equipment-only heat pump permits, a small sample, carry a median of $18,096. Replacing equipment needs a permit; a repair does not.

What decides the cost of heat pump repair in Chicago?

SHORT ANSWER

Four things decide the bill: which part failed, whether the sealed system has to be opened, how hard the outdoor unit is to reach, and which refrigerant the system holds. City & Suburban gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees once the diagnosis is done, and prices the repair against the age of the equipment before recommending it.

Two heat pumps with the same symptom can carry very different repair costs. One sits on a concrete pad in a Niles back yard, with a hose bib ten feet away. The other sits on a flat roof in Wicker Park, reached through a hatch, with a line set running three stories down an outside wall. Same part, different day of work.

Flat rate books price the part and the labor. That works for a capacitor and fails for anything brazed, because the real cost sits in recovery, nitrogen purge, vacuum and a weighed recharge. Quotes that skip those steps are cheaper on paper and shorter lived in the yard. A sealed system opened without a proper vacuum traps moisture that kills the compressor later.

The variable that moved recently is refrigerant. Systems built in the last few years ship with a new blend, which needs its own gauges, recovery machine and tanks. Older systems run on a blend that is still sold, but its supply is being cut back and the price has climbed. The nameplate now changes the cost of the very same repair.

City & Suburban diagnoses first, then quotes upfront with no hidden fees, so the price is known before the work starts. On an older system the repair is priced beside an air conditioning installation quote. The age of the unit and the cost of the fix go into that comparison, so the choice is not a guess. A satisfaction guarantee covers the work either way.

City permit data marks the far end of that scale. In the 24 months to August 2026 Chicago recorded 81 single-scope furnace replacements at a median declared value of $6,807. Equipment-only heat pump permits ran to a median of $18,096. Repair, diagnosis and refrigerant work need no permit at all, so the invoice is the only record a homeowner keeps.

Which Chicago buildings suit a heat pump, and which do not?

SHORT ANSWER

A heat pump suits a Chicago home that already has usable ducts, an outdoor spot for the unit and panel capacity for the circuit. Buildings with steam or hot water heat and no ducts are better served by ductless equipment. City & Suburban looks at the building first, because the building decides the system more often than the budget does.

Chicago housing is old, and it was not built around ducts. A 1920s two-flat heats with steam and has no return air path at all. A brick bungalow has a basement furnace and ducts that were added later. A condo in a 1960s high rise may share a rooftop unit with a neighbor, on a riser nobody is allowed to touch.

Site visits often skip the building. A load calculation gets run off square footage, equipment gets picked from a table, and the crew finds the problem on install day. In a two-flat or a condo conversion that problem is usually the duct path, the electrical panel, or the spot where the outdoor unit was supposed to go.

The constraint that settles most of these jobs is not heating capacity. It is where the outdoor unit can sit, and how the refrigerant lines reach it. Flat roofs, four foot side yards, rear porches and alley setbacks all narrow the options. Where no duct path exists at all, ductless mini-splits solve the same problem without ductwork.

City & Suburban surveys the building before quoting: duct condition and static pressure, panel capacity, the outdoor location and the line set route. The company serves 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, from Pilsen and Rogers Park out to Skokie and Des Plaines, so the housing types repeat and the constraints are familiar. When a heat pump does not suit the building, the recommendation says so.

The age of the stock is measurable. Cook County Assessor records show West Chicago township, which covers Wicker Park and West Town, is 83.0% pre-1940. Jefferson township, the bungalow belt, holds 112,923 properties with a median year built of 1927. Buildings that old were heated long before central cooling existed, so nearly every heat pump in them is a retrofit.

  • Two-flats and greystones with steam heat: no duct path, so ductless equipment fits better
  • Condos with a rooftop or balcony unit: association rules and the line set route decide it
  • Rehabs and condo conversions with new ducts: good candidates, since duct sizing is known
  • Homes with a sound gas furnace: a dual-fuel pairing keeps the furnace for the coldest nights
  • Buildings with no outdoor space and no roof access: the unit location, not the load, is the blocker

COOLING PROBLEMS

When a Heat Pump Stops Cooling Properly

A heat pump cooling problem can begin at the controls, airflow path, or refrigerant circuit. The same warm room can have several causes. These signs help describe the problem when requesting service; safe observations do not replace a diagnosis.

Warm air with the thermostat set to cool Call today

Likely causes

  • Thermostat mode or control setting
  • Restricted indoor airflow
  • Refrigerant or reversing valve fault

Check safely first

  • Confirm the displayed mode is cool.
  • Check the accessible filter without opening equipment panels.
  • Note whether the problem followed a switch from heating.

What the technician does

A technician measures supply-to-return air temperature, checks airflow, and compares refrigerant pressures with operating conditions. Valve control voltage and pipe temperatures distinguish a mode-change fault. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Request service today; appointment timing depends on the schedule.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Air moves, but the home cools very slowly Book soon

Likely causes

  • Dirty filter or blocked return path
  • Reduced heat transfer at the outdoor unit
  • Refrigerant loss or an equipment mismatch

Check safely first

  • Check for a visibly dirty filter.
  • Keep supply and return grilles clear of furniture.
  • Record which rooms stay warm and when the problem occurs.

What the technician does

A technician measures airflow and the indoor temperature drop, then checks outdoor coil condition and refrigerant pressures. These readings distinguish restricted heat transfer from a charge problem. Book an assessment if cooling remains weak after safe checks.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Ice appears on the refrigerant line or indoor coil Call today

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow across the evaporator coil
  • Refrigerant problem
  • Control or airflow fault

Check safely first

  • Stop cooling at the thermostat.
  • Inspect the accessible filter only.
  • Observe visible ice without removing panels.
  • Leave the ice to thaw; do not chip it.

What the technician does

After the ice thaws, a technician measures airflow across the evaporator coil and checks refrigerant pressures and line temperatures. Those readings separate a restriction from a charge or control fault. Stop cooling now and request service; repair time depends on the cause.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Cooling stops after a heating-to-cooling change Call today

Likely causes

  • Incorrect thermostat configuration
  • Reversing valve control fault
  • Mechanical reversing valve problem

Check safely first

  • Confirm cool mode on the thermostat display.
  • Note the previous operating mode.
  • Avoid repeated changes between heating and cooling.

What the technician does

A technician measures the thermostat output and voltage at the reversing valve solenoid. Pipe temperatures show whether refrigerant flow changed, separating a control fault from a mechanical valve problem. Request a visit if the system still delivers warm air in cool mode.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Water collects near the indoor equipment Call today

Likely causes

  • Blocked condensate drainage
  • Ice melting from the evaporator coil
  • Drain connection or collection problem

Check safely first

  • Stop cooling if water is spreading.
  • Keep clear of wet electrical equipment.
  • Observe the source from a dry, accessible location.

What the technician does

A technician traces the condensate path, tests drain flow, and inspects the pan and connections. Coil condition and airflow readings help establish whether melting ice caused the water. Arrange service promptly to limit further water damage.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
The outdoor unit stays quiet while indoor air moves Call today

Likely causes

  • Outdoor electrical or control fault
  • Safety control interruption
  • Thermostat communication problem

Check safely first

  • Confirm cooling is requested on the thermostat.
  • Observe the outdoor unit from a safe distance.
  • Record any displayed error message.

What the technician does

A technician measures incoming voltage and checks the cooling signal, safety controls, and contactor response. Motor current helps distinguish an electrical interruption from a failed outdoor component. Request service if cooling does not resume; do not open electrical panels.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
The heat pump starts and stops repeatedly Book soon

Likely causes

  • Control or thermostat issue
  • Airflow restriction
  • Equipment protection response

Check safely first

  • Note how often operation stops.
  • Inspect the accessible filter.
  • Check that grilles are unobstructed.
  • Record any error message without resetting the system repeatedly.

What the technician does

A technician compares cycle duration with cooling demand and checks thermostat signals, airflow, and fault history. Refrigerant pressures help identify a protection shutdown rather than normal staging. Book service if frequent cycling continues or room temperatures rise.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
A new vibration or grinding noise develops Call today

Likely causes

  • Loose or vibrating assembly
  • Debris or an outdoor fan problem
  • Mechanical wear

Check safely first

  • Stop cooling if the noise is severe.
  • Record the sound from a safe distance.
  • Note whether it occurs at startup or throughout operation.
  • Keep hands and objects outside the equipment.

What the technician does

A technician locates the vibration, checks mounting points and fan clearance, and measures motor current. The source and timing distinguish a loose assembly from mechanical wear. Stop for severe noise and request service; mild persistent vibration also needs attention.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
The home feels damp even while air is cool Book soon

Likely causes

  • Short cooling cycles
  • Airflow or control mismatch
  • Cooling demand beyond current operating conditions

Check safely first

  • Note whether the problem affects the entire home.
  • Check that the thermostat fan setting matches the equipment instructions.
  • Keep vents clear.
  • Record whether dampness is worse after short cooling cycles.

What the technician does

A technician measures indoor humidity, airflow, and cooling cycle duration. The temperature drop across the coil helps distinguish poor moisture removal from a control or airflow mismatch. Book a cooling assessment if dampness persists during normal operation.

Heat Pump Cooling Service Questions

Why does a heat pump blow warm air in cooling mode?

Warm air can reflect a thermostat setting, restricted airflow, a refrigerant problem, or a reversing valve that has not changed modes. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. A service request should include whether the problem began after a mode change or developed during steady summer operation.

Does a heat pump need refrigerant added every summer?

A heat pump should not need a routine summer refrigerant refill. Low refrigerant calls for an assessment of the cause, including a possible leak. Adding refrigerant without addressing the cause can leave the cooling problem unresolved. The refrigerant type and repair scope affect the next steps.

Can a reversing valve problem look like an AC failure?

Yes. A heat pump uses a reversing valve to change the direction of refrigerant flow between heating and cooling. A control problem or valve fault can prevent that change. Warm airflow alone does not identify a failed valve; the settings, airflow, and operating conditions also need attention.

Can central AC be replaced with a heat pump?

A ducted heat pump can be considered when replacing central AC, but the indoor equipment, controls, and ducts must suit the proposed system. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment. A replacement discussion should distinguish the cooling project from the separate plan for winter heating.

What should a summer heat pump service request include?

Useful details include the model, current thermostat mode, rooms affected, visible ice or water, and when cooling last worked normally. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows. Roof access or locked equipment areas should be mentioned when arranging a visit.

Is heat pump maintenance the same as AC maintenance?

The cooling side shares airflow, heat-transfer, and drainage concerns with an air conditioner. A heat pump also changes between cooling and heating modes. Seasonal service should account for the complete system. City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch, and member discounts.

Should a frozen heat pump keep running to cool the home?

Continued cooling operation can add ice and reduce airflow further. Stop cooling and arrange service rather than chipping ice or handling refrigerant connections. A homeowner can note the filter condition and blocked vents. Ice alone does not prove that refrigerant is low or identify the repair needed.

What determines the cost of heat pump cooling repair?

The fault, component availability, refrigerant type, equipment access, and condition of the indoor and outdoor equipment affect the repair scope. City & Suburban offers upfront pricing with no hidden fees. A symptom such as weak cooling does not establish a price before the cause is known.

Does poor cooling mean the heat pump needs replacement?

Poor cooling alone does not justify replacement. A correctable airflow or control issue differs from recurring refrigerant leaks or several major faults. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Compare the identified repair with the condition and compatibility of the complete system before deciding.

Where are winter heating and ductless options explained?

Winter capacity and backup heating require a separate discussion from summer cooling performance. The Heat Pump Heating card links to that decision. Homes considering room-based equipment can follow the Ductless Options card for the alternative to distributing air through existing ducts.

SUMMER PERFORMANCE AND SERVICE

Heat pump cooling in Chicago: service, repair and summer performance

By the City & Suburban team · Reviewed by Rob, owner of City & Suburban · Updated October 2026 · 18 min read

In this guide

  1. How does a heat pump cool a Chicago home in summer?
  2. Why would a heat pump blow warm air in the middle of summer?
  3. What goes wrong with a reversing valve, and how is one tested?
  4. Why does refrigerant charge matter more on a heat pump than on an air conditioner?
  5. What should a heat pump service call include in cooling season?
  6. How often does a heat pump need service when it runs all year?
  7. Should a Chicago home replace central air with a heat pump?
  8. What decides the cost of heat pump repair in Chicago?
  9. Which Chicago buildings suit a heat pump, and which do not?
Book Heat Pump Service Call (773) 238-3838

A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run in reverse. In summer it cools a Chicago home the way central air does, through the same compressor, the same coils and the same ductwork. That shared hardware is why a heat pump which stops cooling in July is a cooling problem, not a heating problem. It is also why the summer faults are specific: a reversing valve that will not shift, a charge that was set in the wrong mode, a defrost board that holds the outdoor fan off. This guide covers what a heat pump needs in cooling season, what Chicago buildings allow, and what switching from central air to a heat pump really changes.

Key takeaways

  • In cooling mode a heat pump is an air conditioner: same compressor, same refrigerant, same ductwork, with a reversing valve added.
  • Warm air in summer usually means one of three things: a stuck reversing valve, a low refrigerant charge, or a control signal that never called for cooling.
  • A heat pump never gets an idle season and runs more hours heating than cooling, so it needs service twice a year.
  • Charge accuracy matters more on a heat pump, because the same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions.
  • City & Suburban repairs heat pumps of all makes and models, installs American Standard equipment, and measures before quoting a part.

How does a heat pump cool a Chicago home in summer?

SHORT ANSWER

In cooling mode a heat pump works like central air. The compressor moves refrigerant, the indoor coil takes heat out of house air, and the outdoor coil dumps that heat outside. The one extra part is a reversing valve, which sets the direction of flow. That valve, the charge and the airflow all have to be tested on a summer call, because all three can look like a dead compressor. City & Suburban repairs heat pumps of all makes and models.

Most Chicago homes with a heat pump got one the same way. An older system came out, and a heat pump went back in on the same pad. Some condos and gut rehabs added cooling where no gas line was available. Either way the outdoor unit sits where the old equipment sat, often on a flat roof or in a narrow side yard between two buildings.

The usual summer call starts with a homeowner who assumes a heat pump is a heating machine. So the search is for a heating company. A technician arrives, checks the indoor furnace side, finds nothing wrong and leaves a service charge behind. Meanwhile the real fault sits in a cooling circuit that nobody measured. Two visits get billed for one problem.

What changed is that the heating and cooling sides are no longer separate boxes. One compressor, one charge and one coil set now serve both seasons, so a summer symptom can come from a winter part. A defrost board that fails stuck can hold the outdoor fan off in July. A valve solenoid that sticks halfway sends some hot gas back indoors. Neither part exists on a plain air conditioner.

A no-cooling heat pump call is a refrigeration diagnosis first. The order that works confirms the mode, then reads suction and liquid pressure. Superheat, subcooling and the temperature drop across the indoor coil follow. Those four numbers separate a valve fault from a charge fault from an airflow fault. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models and gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees, so the part is named once the readings agree.

Cook County Assessor records for the eight Chicago townships show 133,080 houses and small multi-family buildings with central air, and 306,261 without it. Cooling is the newer system in most of this housing stock. A heat pump is the version that lands where a second machine will not fit, so heat pump work here is mostly retrofit work.

Why would a heat pump blow warm air in the middle of summer?

SHORT ANSWER

Warm air from a heat pump in July has three common causes. The reversing valve never shifted into cooling, the refrigerant charge is low, or the control signal asked for heat. The first check belongs at the valve itself. A system stuck in heating will run, draw normal current and sound fine while it quietly warms the house. The call tends to come on the first hot weekend. The thermostat reads 78 degrees, the outdoor unit is running, and air is moving at the registers. That air is room temperature or warmer, and nothing sounds broken. In a Lincoln Park condo with a rooftop unit, the homeowner often cannot even see the equipment to tell whether it is running at all.

The common response is to add refrigerant. A low charge does cause weak cooling, so gauges go on, gas goes in, and the system cools a little better for a week. Nothing was leak tested and nothing was weighed. The charge is now wrong in both modes, which costs the homeowner a second visit and a compressor working harder than it should.

The mechanism most often missed is where the valve rests. On nearly every home heat pump the valve is powered for one mode and relaxed for the other, and the maker decides which. A failed solenoid coil, a broken control wire or a thermostat set up as a conventional system leaves the valve in its resting state. The machine then heats on a cooling call, quite happily.

What goes wrong with a reversing valve, and how is one tested?

SHORT ANSWER

A reversing valve fails in three ways. The solenoid coil dies, the inner slide sticks between positions, or the valve leaks hot gas across its own ports. All three are worth testing before the part is quoted, since the valve body is brazed into the line set. Replacing one means recovering the charge, cutting the unit open and starting again on vacuum. The valve sits on the outdoor unit, a brass cylinder about the size of a fist, with four copper tubes and a small coil on top. Chicago weather is hard on it. Road salt, standing water at a flat roof drain and ten winters of freeze and thaw all work on the coil and its wiring. Winter performance and backup heat sit on the heat pumps page; summer faults are the subject here.

A valve is often condemned on symptoms alone. The system does not cool, the valve is the exotic part, so a quote appears for a valve and a full charge. If the slide was only sticking, the real fault was dirt or a pressure imbalance. The new valve will stick too, and the homeowner has paid for refrigerant twice.

A sticking slide moves on pressure difference, not on magnetism. The solenoid shifts a small pilot valve, and the pressure the compressor makes does the real work. So a weak compressor, a low charge or a restriction can leave a healthy valve halfway across. The test has to separate magnetic force from pressure, which is why the order of checks matters more than the parts list.

The coil gets checked for resistance and for a magnetic field with the circuit live. A light tap on the valve body while the system runs shows whether the slide completes its travel. A valve that bypasses internally sends hot discharge gas straight into the suction port. The common suction line then runs abnormally warm, within a few degrees of the discharge line, while the coil-to-valve tube stays cold. Why does refrigerant charge matter more on a heat pump than on an air conditioner?

SHORT ANSWER

The same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions, so a heat pump has less room for a wrong charge. Weighing refrigerant in beats topping off by pressure, and superheat and subcooling confirm the result in the mode the system is running. A charge set by feel in one season reads wrong in the other. A Chicago heat pump runs far more hours heating than cooling, and it never gets an idle season. The outdoor coil is a condenser in July and an evaporator in January. The indoor evaporator coil swaps roles the same way. Every joint in that circuit sees both pressure extremes and both temperature extremes, year after year.

Charging by pressure alone is still common. Gauges go on, the numbers get compared to a sticker, and gas is added until the suction pressure looks familiar. That method tolerates some error on a cooling-only system. On a heat pump it stacks two errors, because the metering device and the accumulator behave differently in each mode.

The part most often skipped is the path refrigerant takes in reverse. A heat pump carries extra check valves to route flow around the metering device when the mode changes. A stuck check valve, a plugged distributor or a blocked filter drier reads like a charge problem while the charge is correct. Adding gas then makes the numbers worse, not better.

Correct practice recovers the charge, weighs it, and recharges to the amount the maker states, with the leak found before any gas goes in. The constraint that settles most of these jobs is not heating capacity. It is where the outdoor unit can sit, and how the refrigerant lines reach it. contentFields.value: A valve is often condemned on symptoms alone. The system does not cool, the valve is the exotic part, so a quote appears for a valve and a full charge. If the slide was only sticking, the real fault was dirt or a pressure imbalance. The new valve will stick too, and the homeowner has paid for refrigerant twice.

contentFields.label: P: A sticking slide moves on pressure difference, not on magnetism. The solenoid shifts a sma
contentFields.value: A sticking slide moves on pressure difference, not on magnetism. The solenoid shifts a small pilot valve, and the pressure the compressor makes does the real work. So a weak compressor, a low charge or a restriction can leave a healthy valve halfway across. The test has to separate magnetic force from pressure, which is why the order of checks matters more than the parts list.

contentFields.value: The coil gets checked for resistance and for a magnetic field with the circuit live. A light tap on the valve body while the system runs shows whether the slide completes its travel. A valve that bypasses internally sends hot discharge gas straight into the suction port. The common suction line then runs abnormally warm, within a few degrees of the discharge line, while the coil-to-valve tube stays cold. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting, so a valve is replaced only when those readings condemn it, and the charge is weighed back in afterward.

contentFields.label: H3: Why does refrigerant charge matter more on a heat pump than on an air conditioner?
contentFields.value: Why does refrigerant charge matter more on a heat pump than on an air conditioner?

contentFields.label: P: The same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions, so a heat pump has less roo
contentFields.value: The same refrigerant has to meter correctly in two directions, so a heat pump has less room for a wrong charge. Weighing refrigerant in beats topping off by pressure, and superheat and subcooling confirm the result in the mode the system is running. A charge set by feel in one season reads wrong in the other. City & Suburban diagnoses before quoting.

contentFields.label: P: A Chicago heat pump runs far more hours heating than cooling, and it never gets an idle se
contentFields.value: A Chicago heat pump runs far more hours heating than cooling, and it never gets an idle season. The outdoor coil is a condenser in July and an evaporator in January. The indoor evaporator coil swaps roles the same way. Every joint in that circuit sees both pressure extremes and both temperature extremes, year after year.

contentFields.label: P: Charging by pressure alone is still common. Gauges go on, the numbers get compared to a st
contentFields.value: Charging by pressure alone is still common. Gauges go on, the numbers get compared to a sticker, and gas is added until the suction pressure looks familiar. That method tolerates some error on a cooling-only system. On a heat pump it stacks two errors, because the metering device and the accumulator behave differently in each mode.

contentFields.label: P: The part most often skipped is the path refrigerant takes in reverse. A heat pump carries
contentFields.value: The part most often skipped is the path refrigerant takes in reverse. A heat pump carries extra check valves to route flow around the metering device when the mode changes. A stuck check valve, a plugged distributor or a blocked filter drier reads like a charge problem while the charge is correct. Adding gas then makes the numbers worse, not better.

contentFields.label: P: Refrigerant work is also the least documented part of the trade. A City of Chicago permit
contentFields.value: Refrigerant work is also the least documented part of the trade. A City of Chicago permit is required to replace equipment, but repair, diagnosis, maintenance and refrigerant work need none. Of 62,810 permits issued in the 24 months to August 2026, only 4,888 mention HVAC work at all. Nothing outside the shop's own method checks a charge, which is why the numbers belong on the invoice.

contentFields.value: A cooling season heat pump visit should cover both halves of the machine. That means mode and valve operation, charge by measurement, airflow across the indoor coil, electrical draw, and the defrost control that only runs in winter. A thorough visit works through that whole list instead of stopping at the first fault. City & Suburban gives upfront pricing with no hidden fees before any part is ordered.

contentFields.value: From the driveway, a heat pump call in August looks like an air conditioning call. The difference is in what gets left alone. A cooling-only visit never touches a defrost board, an outdoor sensor or a backup heat relay, because those parts are not there. A heat pump paired with an air handler has no gas side at all, so the whole visit is refrigeration and electrical.

contentFields.value: Many summer visits stop at the first fault that explains the symptom. A dirty filter gets changed, cooling comes back, and the invoice closes. Three weeks later the capacitor that was already reading low takes the compressor off line during a heat wave. The second call costs more than the first, and it arrives at the worst time of the year.

contentFields.value: What changes the math is run hours. A cooling-only system in Chicago runs a few hundred hours a year. A heat pump runs in both seasons, so the compressor, contactor, capacitor and outdoor fan motor age at roughly twice the rate. Parts that would have outlived an air conditioner now wear out mid life, which makes the electrical readings as important as the refrigerant ones.

contentFields.value: How often does a heat pump need service when it runs all year?

contentFields.value: A heat pump should be serviced twice a year, once before cooling season and once before heating season. It builds up roughly double the run hours of a cooling-only system. contentFields.value: An air conditioner in Chicago gets one tune-up in spring and then sits idle for seven months. A heat pump never sits idle. It switches modes in October and again in April. The outdoor coil collects cottonwood in May, grass clippings in July and leaves in November, so the cabinet is never clean for long.

contentFields.value: The default is to treat the machine as an air conditioner and book one spring visit. That visit washes the outdoor coil, checks the charge and closes. contentFields.value: The better split is by mode rather than by season name. A spring visit has to prove cooling capacity and clear the condensate path. contentFields.value: Flat rate books price the part and the labor. contentFields.value: The variable that moved recently is refrigerant. Systems built in the last few years ship with a new blend, which needs its own gauges, recovery machine and tanks.
